title: Show HN: Aroha – signed, shrinking permissions for AI agents, checked offline
story_key: story|title:aroha signed shrinking permissions for ai agents checked offline
content_excerpt: Aroha Mandates let any agent that delegates keep cryptographically enforceable control over every agent it hands work to. No agent can exceed the scope it was granted. Agents now act for people and hand work to other agents and tools, often run by other companies. MCP and A2A connect them; identity providers name them. Nothing that travels with the work proves what each agent was allowed to do, stops the whole chain when the person changes their mind, or leaves a record anyone else can check. Aroha answers four questions for every action: who is acting, what were they allowed to do, can it be stopped, and what actually happened. It works with MCP, A2A and your identity provider rather than replacing them. See what Aroha is (and is not) . Using an AI coding agent? Point it at the aroha-integrate Agent Skill (or docs/llms.txt ): it picks the smallest integration path for your code, applies it, and checks that out-of-scope calls are refused. Note: the Vercel and Cloudflare buttons clone from github.com/ArohaLabs/aroha-protocol . You can also copy the template directory from a checkout and deploy it with the platform CLI. The Aroha runtime (desktop app) is developed in a separate, private repository and has not been released. The saga, settlement, commerce and reputation extensions are also developed outside this repository; they stay published on npm. Foundry and Python are only needed for the smart contract demo and MkDocs docs site respectively. Use GitHub Issues for bugs and feature requests and GitHub Discussions for questions and ideas, or email the maintainer listed in MAINTAINERS.md . See CONTRIBUTING.md (commits need a DCO sign-off) and SUPPORT.md . For security issues, see SECURITY.md .

title: Paradev: One workspace for Claude Code, Codex, and any coding agent
story_key: model:claude code|title:paradev one workspace for claude code codex and any coding agent
content_excerpt: ● Two changes. Cap the query at MAX_QUERY_LENGTH and return didOverflow so callers can show a hint. Use Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, or any coding agent for each task. Your workspaces, branches, and review flow stay the same. Launch agents across features, bug fixes, and refactors, all in parallel. Status at a glance shows which agents are working, which are blocked, and which are waiting on you. Turn chores into agents that run on a schedule or when an event comes in: issue triage, changelog drafts, dependency bumps. They run on their own and open PRs for you to review. Each agent runs in its own isolated Git worktree. No overwriting each other's files. Review and merge work when you're ready. Add any machine as a host. Workspaces keep running when your laptop sleeps, and you can check in from wherever you are. Everything is scriptable. Spawn workspaces and agents from the CLI, wire Paradev into CI with the SDK, or let your agent drive it over MCP. Jump into your favorite editor with one click. VS Code, Cursor, Xcode, JetBrains IDEs, or any terminal: open worktrees exactly where you need them. Oh snap @superset_sh is soooooo damn good! Now THIS is the experience I've been wanting for CLI agents! Damn @superset_sh is really cool. You should try it. worktrees are a breeze cmd + t auto opens Claude Code you can view git changes within itself closing a laptop doesn't kill the sessions If you prefer a more GUI-oriented approach to multiple agents in parallel, it seems like @superset_sh is doing a tremendous job. @superset_sh is a sick product - love OS since I don't have to wait for someone else to fix bugs hasn't been a day i haven't used superset since onboarding complete paradigm shift on how i use ai to code Tested various GUI tools for git worktree and agents - Conductor, Vibe Kanban, Agentastic, Crystal, FleetCode, Emdash, Sculptor - but Paradev suits my taste the best just started using remote desktop instead of ssh just to be able to use @superset_sh on my mac mini from my macbook pro generational product in the making, mark my words Your code stays local by default, with explicit control over connected services. Full source available on GitHub under Elastic License 2.0 (ELv2). Inspect, audit, and contribute to the code. No black boxes, no hidden functionality. Repos, worktrees, terminal output, and agent sessions stay on your machine. Cloud sync covers account and organization metadata only. Use your existing agent subscriptions and API keys. Paradev

title: Show HN: Agent outputs slop texts, so I make a superfast HTML skill visualize it
story_key: story|title:agent outputs slop texts so i make a superfast html skill visualize it
content_excerpt: Answer me with HTML — an agent skill that answers hard questions with a one-page HTML you can actually read. 让 AI Agent 用一页 HTML 回答复杂问题。 An agent skill. Ask a hard question, get a page you can actually read instead of a wall of text. The model writes about 1/8 of the tokens it would need to hand-write the HTML. The agent writes a short Markdown draft and hands it to the CLI that ships with the skill. About 50 ms later you have a page: You can. Models write decent HTML now. But most of what they write is not content. We counted the tokens in 9 pages the model wrote by hand, 4,893 tokens on average: With this skill the model writes only a Markdown draft. For the same questions that was 612 tokens on average, about 1/8 of the hand-written HTML . Less to write means less to wait for (3 topics × 3 runs, medians, Claude Sonnet 5.5, a plain Claude Code setup): The token counts are saved in bench/corpus/tokens.json , so node bench/corpus.mjs gives the same numbers every time. The pages themselves are a download . The bill drops less than the writing, about 15% here, because every turn also reads the system prompt, your question and the conversation, with or without the skill. See where the cost goes . Explainer videos save even more: about 18× fewer output tokens and 12× faster in a small test . You need Node.js 20 or newer. There is no npm install step. The CLI is bundled inside the skill. No Node.js yet? With the recommended install below, your agent asks you and then installs it. Install Answer me with HTML: read https://raw.githubusercontent.com/QingYunA/answer-me-with-html/main/INSTALL.md and follow it. INSTALL.md is written for agents. It installs the plugin in Claude Code and the skill in other agents, keeps an existing install, asks you nothing unless Node.js is missing or older than 20, and ends with one report after checking the result with the TCP three-way handshake page. If your agent cannot open links, use npx -y skills add QingYunA/answer-me-with-html -g -y -a <your agent name> (for Claude Code, -a claude-code ). It asks which agents to install into. The installer, vercel-labs/skills , supports more than 70 agents. Copy the skills/answer-me-with-html folder into your agent's skill folder. For Claude Code: Skill folders for other agents: Codex ~/.codex/skills/ , Cursor ~/.cursor/skills/ , OpenCode ~/.config/opencode/skill/ . No setup is needed after install. title: CoSA: The Conflict of Skills Attack in Real-World LLM Agent Ecosystems
summary: Agent Skills allow LLM agents to combine reusable capabilities, but checking each Skill in isolation cannot rule out policy violations when they are composed. We term such failures Conflict of Skills (CoS): artifacts or assessment signals produced for one purpose may be reused downstream without preserving the restrictions or authorization needed for their new use. Using controlled executions of publicly available Skills and matched single-Skill controls, we identify four recurring mechanisms behind CoS. Building on these findings, we introduce the Conflict of Skills Attack (CoSA), which adds locally admitted Skills to an existing pool to supply missing business operations (capability supplementation) or reshape artifact exchange, decision reuse, and target/action bindings (relationship reshaping). CoSA leaves existing Skills and runtime permissions unchanged. To evaluate this threat under autonomous Skill selection, we introduce CoSA-Bench, built from real-world Skills and controlled services, with 288 tasks across recruiting, finance, IT, and business, covering data leakage, unauthorized state modification, and unsafe execution. Across five LLMs and three agent harnesses, additions capped at 5% of each original pool raise the policy-violation rate from 35.02% to 58.45%, an increase of 23.43 percentage points. Trace analysis links compliant-to-violating transitions to cross-Skill dependencies involving the additions. Finally, we develop a lightweight harness-level guard that checks information flow and authorization before consequential actions. On OpenClaw recruiting tasks across five models, the guard reduces violations from 65.28% to 6.67%, while policy-compliant task completion on matched benign controls changes from 66.67% to 65.00%.

title: BehaviorMem: Building and Evaluating User Memory from Real-World E-Commerce Behavior Streams
summary: User memory helps personalized systems build on their understanding of users over time. In e-commerce, users convey their preferences and needs through both explicit language and implicit interactions with products. We study memory built from logs of these interactions, examining how it can \emph{remember} concrete evidence and established interests, and use that evidence to \emph{infer} underlying needs and preferences that inform judgments beyond well-observed product domains. Existing memory methods primarily target language-based interactions, and evaluations offer limited real behavioral data and limited separation of these capabilities. This leaves open how to jointly support and separately evaluate remembering and inference from behavioral logs. We formulate the problem of continual behavioral user memory around these joint requirements and develop a dedicated evaluation framework and memory method to address them. \textbf{BehaviorMemBench} is a benchmark built from real e-commerce logs covering 1{,}194 users and 17{,}462 behavioral batches over more than three years, with automatic future-behavior labels and a task-independent memory interface to separately evaluate remembering and inference under a common protocol. \textbf{BehaviorMem} is a memory design that organizes explicit behavioral facts and inferred user characteristics across long-term and short-term scopes in a two-axis state, with evidence-grounded formation, continual maintenance, and query-independent readout. Experiments across two builders and two task readers show that BehaviorMem leads the evaluated agentic memories on remember and infer, and reveal different method rankings across the two capabilities and competitive statistical baselines. Validation on a public dataset further supports its usefulness for downstream tasks based on behavioral histories.

title: webframe: evaluated as a scraper and a sandbox
summary:
Research: webframe: evaluated as a scraper and a sandbox

webframe is a neat little project from Jeff Lindsay which lets you "run a web page like a program" - you point it at a URL or file and it executes it in a hidden headless web view and outputs console.log() to standard output and any exceptions to standard error.

It's written in Go on top of the glaze library, which provides access to a system browser ("WKWebView on macOS, WebKitGTK on Linux, WebView2 on Windows") so it doesn't need to bundle its own browser engine.

It reminds me of my own shot-scraper javascript tool, albeit in a much smaller package that doesn't depend on Playwright.

I had Claude Opus 5.5 put it through its paces and prepare a research report for me. Here's the prompt I used:

Explore https://github.com/tractordev/webframe try running it and put it though its paces, build a few exploratory prototypes, then evaluate it as a potential sandboxing tool and as a tool for scraping web pages using the same patterns encouraged by the "shot-scraper JavaScript" command (see simonw/shot-scraper on GitHub, docs directory)

title: The Hitchhiker's Guide to System 1 Models: Fast Decision-Making Beyond LLMS
summary: Large Language Models excel at reasoning and generation but their autoregressive, token-by-token inference makes them unnecessarily slow, expensive, and poorly calibrated for the many routine decisions (routing, gating, scoring, classification) that modern AI systems require at sub-second latency. A growing class of models addresses this gap: System 1 decision models, architectures that map an input directly to a typed, structured decision in a single forward pass. This guide provides a comprehensive, practitioner-oriented treatment of the field. We propose a five-family taxonomy covering encoder-based classifiers, reward models, non-autoregressive decision engines, contrastive decision models, and extraction models, and we provide in-depth coverage of each family's architecture, training methodology, and deployment trade-offs. A central theme is calibration: we develop the theory of proper scoring rules, analyze Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD), and examine recently discovered phenomena including IIA violations, ordinal-scale bias, and few-shot recalibration under distribution shift. On the integration side, we describe how System 1 models serve as decision infrastructure within agentic workflows and System 1 + System 2 cascades that route between fast and slow models based on calibrated confidence. The guide covers 18 application domains, maps the rapidly growing open-source ecosystem (over 70 model reproductions in weeks), provides runnable code throughout, and includes a practitioner's checklist, an open-source model zoo, and 22 self-assessment questions with detailed answers. Spanning 190 references, it is intended as a unified entry point for researchers and engineers working at the intersection of fast decision-making, calibration, and production AI systems.

title: Cross-request KV cache exposure in the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model, and our remediation with SGLang
summary: A configuration mismatch in GLM 5.3 on Workers AI triggered an SGLang bug that exposed KV cache pages across requests. Here is how we addressed the issue.
story_key: model:glm|ver:5.3|title:cross request kv cache exposure in the glm 5 3 workers ai model and our remediat
content_excerpt: On September 8, 2026, we were alerted by a security researcher, Gadi Evron from Knostic, to a tenant isolation issue affecting the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model ( @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 ) starting on August 27, 2026. We have remediated the issue, and we restored the model on September 9. We have confirmed that no other model hosted on Workers AI was affected. Between August 27 and September 9, a small number of customers using the GLM 5.3 Workers AI model received responses that contained data from other customers' requests made to the same model shortly before theirs. In total, 155 responses were affected, all to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens. After excluding our own testing and the researcher's, the requests we identified are consistent in timing and volume with ordinary long-context use, not with someone repeatedly exploiting the bug. We found no evidence of deliberate exploitation. Today we are publishing this report alongside a post from SGLang, the open-source inference engine that we use, as a coordinated disclosure. This post describes the bug that caused this issue, our response timeline, and the subsequent hardening we have conducted on our production SGLang deployments. We also detail our continued efforts with the upstream maintainers of SGLang to address this and similar bugs. GLM is a text generation model from Z.ai that is built for agentic coding workflows; it is one of the many models available through Workers AI. Gadi Evron submitted a report on September 8 through our HackerOne program stating that very long prompts sent to @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 on Workers AI sometimes returned text that belonged to other users' sessions. Cloudflare reproduced the issue the next morning and took the model offline within 40 minutes of declaring an incident. We then deployed a corrected configuration and a patched inference engine, and restored service the same day. This specific report of cross-request KV cache exposure was the result of two overlapping issues. The first was a misconfiguration of the open-source inference engine, SGLang, used by Cloudflare. We deployed GLM 5.3 with a 1,048,576-token context window, but the KV cache pool on our prefill GPUs only had room for 681,280 tokens. We were aware of this mismatch before launch. We expected the engine to return an error for any prompt it could not process, and our long-context tests returned successful responses, so we did not believe this to be an issue. title: claude-code v2.1.311
summary:
What's changed

  • Added --hold-idle-file and --max-hold-min to self-hosted-runner, to keep an idle session while your host reports processes it left running
  • Added a tip for the Explanatory output style, shown when you ask Claude for explanations
  • Fixed long freezes at startup and after reading or editing files when a CLAUDE.md file holds a very long list item
  • Fixed interrupting Claude not taking effect until a timeout while an MCP server had not answered a resource read or a skill was still downloading
  • Fixed standard-context sessions stopping with "Usage credits required for 1M context" when a request ran over 200K tokens; Claude Code now compacts the conversation and continues
  • Fixed Write and Edit stalling for up to 5 seconds after they ran, and reporting 0 lines changed, when changing thousands of lines in a file
  • Fixed subagents being unable to use MCP tools from servers that finish connecting after the subagent starts
  • Fixed Claude seeing stale MEMORY.md and CLAUDE.md content right after automatic compaction when those files were edited earlier in the session
  • Fixed claude -p and SDK sessions saving transcript messages out of order or keeping messages that were taken back
  • Fixed SubagentStop hooks running about twice a minute for each running subagent instead of once when it finishes
  • Fixed the @ file picker ignoring .ignore/.rgignore negation rules that re-include git-ignored files
  • Fixed a subagent's isolated worktree being removed while a background subagent it started was still working in it
  • Fixed background agents in auto mode that wait on their own shells starting a new main conversation turn on every wake
  • Fixed the Bash tool description claiming the working directory always persists between calls
  • Fixed the environment block naming a shell commands don't run in, such as fish when the Bash tool uses zsh
  • Fixed claude mcp add, claude mcp remove and /mcp naming the current folder instead of the project entry in ~/.claude.json that holds a local-scope server when run below a repository root
  • Fixed claude mcp list and claude mcp get showing the error code twice on failed-connection lines (for example ENOENT: ENOENT: …)
  • Fixed Remote Control sessions staying on "Connecting" for about two minutes when a network proxy blocks a startup request
  • Fixed messages that Claude sends to a cloud or Remote Control session appearing as your own message in the Claude mobile apps
  • Fixed Claude not being told the cause when a file attached to a message sent over Remote Control or to a cloud session could not be saved because the disk was full, or that a message's attachments past the first 20 were left out
  • Fixed WebFetch and WebSearch hanging on a stalled response in Cowork cloud sessions; an unfinished request now fails after 300 seconds
  • Fixed a background session that crashed between turns not being restarted while it was attached, pinned, or had a scheduled task or wake-up set
  • Fixed the "background service did not respond" error suggesting the disabled claude daemon restart; it now suggests claude daemon stop --any and says it ends background sessions
  • Fixed claude respawn <id> starting the background service before reporting that no background session matches the id
  • Fixed /effort not warning about a prompt cache miss in plan mode when the plan model differs from the session model
  • Fixed /ide saying the VS Code extension was installed before the install finished or when it failed
  • Fixed the Write tool's file preview skipping rows and miscounting hidden lines when a line is wider than the terminal
  • Fixed ↑ in an agent's chat tab recalling a message that was still waiting to be delivered, so resending it sent a second copy
  • Fixed Cowork cloud sessions losing their connectors and most tools after a restart when a plugin or your settings named an agent; Cowork cloud sessions now ignore that setting
  • Fixed agent teams sessions showing an empty task list when coming back with --resume, --continue, /resume or --session-id, including after /clear or a crash, and /branch writing to the original session's list
  • Fixed pasting text that mentions an image file, such as ! open /tmp/shot.png or /review look at /tmp/shot.png, attaching the image and dropping its path from the prompt
  • Fixed the feedback draft card showing its 1/2/0 and Esc shortcuts while the prompt has text, when those keys act on the prompt instead of the card
  • Fixed a lone backslash in quotes or brackets, like "\" or (\), disappearing from Claude's responses
  • Fixed agent teammates compacting their history when DISABLE_COMPACT is set
  • Fixed the rewind menu offering "Summarize from here" and "Summarize up to here" when DISABLE_COMPACT is set
  • Fixed a finished /code-review, or another skill that runs in a sub-agent, running a second time when a cloud or background session restarts
  • Fixed long hidden thinking being cut off as idle on Google Vertex AI, Microsoft Foundry and Claude Platform on AWS, where the endpoint sends thinking progress updates
  • Fixed /ide saying it had installed the JetBrains plugin when nothing was installed
  • Fixed Claude Pro and Max subscribers being told to ask their admin when their subscription can't be used; the message now points to billing settings
  • Fixed the diff pane opening by itself after an edit in wide fullscreen terminals when it had nothing to show
  • Fixed /mcp showing a remote server as failed after "Clear authentication" when the server works without sign-in
  • Fixed /mcp showing "authenticated" for a remote server that Claude Code sends no credentials to
  • Fixed a --plugin-dir folder of plugins loading as one plugin when an empty .mcp.json was at its top
  • Fixed /usage never showing large prompt-cache misses under "What's contributing to your limits usage?"
  • Fixed status line links staying plain text in background sessions after you open them from a terminal that supports links
  • Fixed the /rewind confirmation saying the conversation "will be forked" when the later messages are removed from the conversation
  • Fixed the /rewind warning that wrongly said manual and Bash edits are never affected by a code restore
  • Fixed plan approval in screen reader mode sending feedback you had dismissed with Escape
  • Fixed Claude Code retrying requests the API marked not to retry, which could hold a turn for minutes or, in unattended retry mode (CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG), indefinitely
  • Linux: Fixed sandboxed Bash commands failing with bwrap: Can't create file when a --plugin-dir folder was also an added directory and permissions.blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories was on
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a session failing to start when a rate limit (HTTP 429, or a git wrapper that exits 75) blocks an added read-only repository; it now starts without that repository
  • Improved startup time for Pro and Max accounts by skipping two network requests on launches within an hour of the last check
  • Improved /teleport and claude --teleport to warn when a compacted cloud session loads from its last compaction, so the messages it summarized aren't in the local copy
  • Improved the messages shown when a background session's process exits: they no longer promise a restart that isn't coming, and they say how to resume the session
  • Improved artifacts with several views: Claude now routes each view on the link's #name and no longer says the address bar stays the same as you switch views
  • Improved shell commands that reach their timeout: the result now shows the output so far and says the command is still running in the background
  • Improved compaction: when the model's reply has no summary in it, Claude Code now usually asks for the summary once more before it replaces the conversation
  • Improved the Artifact tool's choice between a page and a document: explainers and visual or interactive work become artifact pages; documents are for writing people keep editing or pass around
  • Improved startup time for launches whose only arguments are options and their values, such as claude --model opus
  • Improved the "Connection dropped" API error: it now says where to look first (the proxy or gateway in use, else VPN or firewall; Anthropic API only, Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry are unchanged)
  • Improved screen reader mode: deleting a rule in /permissions says "Deleted allow rule …" right away
  • Improved the message shown when a pasted sign-in code is refused: it now says the code may have expired or been used, and to sign in again
  • Improved Slack connector sends: Claude now checks a channel's topic for posting rules before messaging a channel you didn't name
  • Improved screen reader mode: Claude's questions are listed as "Questions: Color (answered), Pages", without arrows or symbols
  • Changed ultrathink in the interactive terminal to run its turn at xhigh effort on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5 and Fable 5.1 through Anthropic's API; typed while Claude is working, it raises the rest of that turn
  • Changed the ultrathink rainbow to appear only where the keyword can raise effort, and not when the word is quoted or part of a file path
  • Changed Ctrl+D in agent view to match the prompt: on an empty input, pressing it twice exits
  • Changed --output-format json and stream-json output to write DEL, C1 control and Unicode format characters inside strings as \uXXXX escapes; parsed values are unchanged
  • Changed model names and IDs to drop the [1m] suffix and its label on models where the suffix has no effect; the suffix is still accepted
  • Changed startup warnings about permission rules in settings files to show once per user until the rule changes
  • Changed /code-review to tell Claude to put the effort level first and use max only when asked
  • Changed DISABLE_COMPACT in settings files and in a mod's $.env.set so they can only turn compaction off, not back on
  • Changed Claude Code on Bedrock, Mantle, Vertex, and Foundry to load model settings from a signed file on downloads.claude.ai; set CLAUDE_CODE_MODEL_CATALOG=off to turn this off
  • Changed sessions that set CLAUDE_CODE_SYNC_SKILLS with feature-flag fetching off to reuse a claude.ai skills list up to 10 minutes old that another session on the machine fetched
  • Changed clicks on scrollbar arrows and bars in fullscreen lists to act when the mouse button is released, so moving off the scrollbar before letting go cancels the click
  • Changed claude purge to say it deletes data only on this computer, not anything stored by Anthropic
  • [VSCode] Added syntax coloring to code blocks in Claude's replies, in light, dark and high contrast dark themes
  • [VSCode] Added a "Running UserPromptSubmit hooks" spinner status and screen reader announcement for slow UserPromptSubmit hooks
  • [VSCode] Fixed custom skills and custom slash commands sent from the VS Code or JetBrains panel leaving out the open file or selected lines that ordinary messages include (#102799)
  • [VSCode] Fixed the extension host freezing while the login shell ran its start-up files to read PATH on macOS and Linux
  • [VSCode] Fixed clicking an image in a tool result, or closing its preview, also opening the result's text in an editor tab
  • [VSCode] Fixed voice dictation continuing to record after a message was sent with the Send button; sending now stops dictation first, as pressing Enter already did
  • [VSCode] Changed the extension to start Claude Code sessions with DISABLE_TELEMETRY set while VS Code's telemetry setting is off, so they send no usage metrics or error reports and fetch no feature flags
  • [VSCode] Changed the session list side bar to load Web sessions when the Web tab is first opened, not at startup
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed routines in Anthropic-hosted environments staying locked after their owner left the organization and rejoined; the owner can now turn them back on
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed a failed routine API token delete or regenerate showing nothing if the edit dialog had already closed; it now shows an error toast
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed cloud environment dialogs, including the admin dialog, accepting duplicate names; they now refuse a name another listed environment already has
  • [Claude Tag] Added a Skills view to Claude Tag analytics showing how often Claude runs each attached skill in Slack channels and which go unused, with Usage links in admin settings
  • [Claude Tag] Improved Claude Tag routines that run in a new session: a run with nothing to report can now end without posting a throwaway message to the channel
  • [Claude Tag] Changed Claude Tag admin settings to show a lock instead of # for private Slack channels that your own Slack account can see
  • [Code Review] Improved Code Review's check run to say no further automatic review will start when the model still can't analyze a change on the automatic retry
  • [Code Review] Improved Code Review reliability: a review whose session fails to start because of a transient server fault is now retried once automatically, and its check run says so

title: Memory or a Clock? Auditing a Memory Advantage in XLand-MiniGrid with Seeds, Maps and Evaluation Noise Apart
summary: On a partially observable XLand-MiniGrid task, an LSTM agent beats a memory-free MLP by 25 percentage points. The gap looks like a clear case of memory. We ask two questions about it. First, how much of a measured gap is noise? Separating training seed, map and evaluation randomness in 60 runs, each re-evaluated three times, we find that about ten paired seeds detect a 10-point gap in final success. The binary "task acquired" verdict, a common summary of learning curves, is 76% evaluation noise and would need about a hundred seeds for the same gap. Second, is the gap memory? On a sealed panel of new maps, opened once, a memory-free MLP of the LSTM's size comes within 3.3 points of the LSTM when it is given the time step, and gains no measurable benefit from its width without it. With the time step, an MLP a quarter of the LSTM's size, and the LSTM with its state erased at every step, also come within about 5 points. A linear probe reads the time step from the trained LSTM's state. On this task, most of the apparent memory advantage is an advantage of knowing the time, which matters because episodes are cut at a fixed limit and the reward shrinks with time. We recommend giving memory-free baselines the time step, and we release the protocol, the event-driven tooling and every checkpoint.

title: The five components of building a "company harness"
summary: Learn how LangChain built internal agents across marketing, sales, and engineering, and how they have completely changed how those teams work.
story_key: story|title:the five components of building a company harness
content_excerpt: We've built internal agents at LangChain across marketing, sales, and engineering, and they have completely changed how those teams work. They weren't easy to get right. We spent a lot of time solving the problems that come with a multiplayer harness, and every team landed on the same core primitives: To ground this discussion, a brief overview of the three main agents we have at LangChain: GTM Agent : a proactive, always-on agent that assists with GTM activities. Monitors and responds to emails, to new qualified leads, sends daily briefs, can answer questions about accounts, can run outbound motions OpenSWE : our engineering agent, can work on and draft PRs, but also runs code review over all PRs Content Studio : our marketing agent, can draft assets (blogs, images, PowerPoints, videos) in our style and with knowledge of our positioning All of these agents are built in the same way. We think this is a general recipe for building company harnesses. All our agents live where people already work, which for us is Slack. They each have their own Slack apps , and can be DM’d or tagged in a channel. One benefit of working with these agents in channels is that others can see how people use it. One nice thing we added was the concept of “breaking” out a conversation in Slack. Oftentimes, a great conversation would be happening and you’d want to add in your agent to get their opinion or get them to do something. But if they ran in that thread it would pollute the human conversation and distract. So we added an easy way for agents to “breakout” into their own thread in the channel. There are some user experiences that are best NOT done in Slack. For example, when reviewing emails GTM Agent wants me to send, it's fine to do that in a one-off way in Slack, but if there is a big backlog it's not a fun experience at all to track those from Slack messages. For experiences like that, we did end up building a custom UI. The thorniest and trickiest problem we tackled was identity, specifically: when these agents take actions, who do they take actions on behalf of? This is how we handled it for each agent (docs: Add identity to Managed Deep Agents , Manage connections ): This is probably the least explored area so far - we have a lot of work we want to do here! All three of our agents can write and execute code, and often need to in order to accomplish tasks. title: Ensemble forecasting with IBM Granite time-series models
story_key: story|title:ensemble forecasting with ibm granite time series models
content_excerpt: Four open Granite models, one extensible forecasting interface, and less guesswork about which model to use. Pre-trained time-series models can forecast without training on your dataset, but you still have to choose one. A model that handles smooth industrial signals well may struggle with noisy retail demand or a long seasonal horizon, and the best choice depends on the series and the task. Granite Timeseries Ensemble reduces that choice to a sensible default. One recipe combines four complementary Granite architectures and returns median and quantile forecasts, with no retraining and no fitted ensemble weights. Start with the Probabilistic Ensemble (uniform probability pooling), compare the adaptive Inter Quartile Range (IQR) Ensemble, and extend the same interface with compatible forecasters. The ensemble recipe and its default Granite members are permissively licensed. The idea will be familiar from weather forecasting. Ensemble forecasts explore a range of possible outcomes, and systems such as the North American Multi-Model Ensemble combine different models for seasonal prediction. Time-series forecasting benefits in a similar way: complementary models offer different views of what comes next, and an ensemble merges those views into one forecast. Install Granite TSFM and load the recommended four-model recipe directly from Hugging Face: The recipe stores the ensemble configuration rather than merged model weights. It downloads the four member checkpoints at runtime, so allow extra time for the first run. For the full configuration, member checkpoints, evaluation details, and limitations, see the model card . result.prediction_outputs contains the point forecast, while result.quantile_outputs contains the quantile predictions which by default range from 0.1 to 0.9. Applications can use the point value as a central prediction and selected quantiles to express forecast ranges. For example, the 0.1 and 0.9 quantiles define a central forecast interval with nominal 80% coverage. The default recipe combines four pre-trained Granite models with different architectures: For background, see the PatchTST-FM-r1 paper , PatchTST-FM-r2 architecture overview , FlowState paper , and Tiny Time Mixers paper . These architectures capture trends, seasonality, and local variation in different ways, so their errors need not coincide. title: NVIDIA Vera CPUs double throughput for Modal Sandboxes
summary: We benchmarked NVIDIA's new Arm-based Vera CPU on agentic Sandbox workloads. Under heavy load, it completes far more tasks than the x86 and Graviton alternatives, without sacrificing latency.
story_key: model:modal|title:nvidia vera cpus double throughput for modal sandboxes
content_excerpt: Last week, NVIDIA hand-delivered Modal’s first Vera CPU server to our SF office. It’s now purring away in a server rack, and we’re pretty excited about what it could mean for Modal Sandboxes and, consequently, Modal users. Vera is NVIDIA’s new Arm-compatible CPU, built for the Vera Rubin GPU platform but also available as a standalone CPU server. Supporting Arm would be a huge change for Modal, coming from a long history exclusively running x86 machines. We’d need to make changes across our infrastructure and image build system to support an entirely different CPU architecture, but the benchmarks are impressive: a 2x increase on throughput. With this, the NVIDIA Vera CPU becomes an incredibly compelling option for powering Modal Sandboxes. Orchestration for a Sandbox product means running hundreds of concurrent containers and VMs on each cloud host. Unlike normal Kubernetes server deployments colocating pods on the same host, the shape of each sandbox workload is unique, and it leads to some interesting dynamics within a multi-tenant cluster: As a result of this, it’s incredibly difficult for users to know how to size their workloads, and for Modal to schedule them without contention. Unlike other providers that force users to choose fixed reservations for max usage, Modal Sandboxes support bursting , which allows users to reserve guaranteed capacity for their P50 usage, rather than the worst-case P100 npm install moment, and trust when the transient spike comes along it’d be absorbed by the padding within the host node. It’s a great strategy, and we’ve saved users millions of dollars teaching them to trust burstability, but it increases exposure to noisy neighbor issues otherwise avoided by strict limits. Sandboxes are usually run to augment some external process, and that process bottlenecking on the CPU leads to real dollars spent. At Modal, we see two prevalent use cases: background agents and reinforcement learning rollouts. To test Vera, we built a set of representative workloads and benchmarks for agentic Sandboxes. Creating an “agentic” benchmark is a challenging task, given most of the work done on the servers is not CPU bound, and there’s no specific dimension we’d want to optimize for. Where a DB workload could optimize for disk I/O and an image processing workload could optimize SIMD, for sandboxes we needed to come up with a simulator that is both concurrent and heterogeneous: a big ol’ bag of chaos we could throw at the CPU. title: Introducing vLLM TorchTPU
summary: vllm-torchtpu is a new vLLM backend for Google Cloud TPUs built on TorchTPU, with Pallas kernels, multi-host parallelism, KV cache offloading, and disaggregated serving.
story_key: model:vllm|title:introducing vllm torchtpu
content_excerpt: Today we're releasing vLLM TorchTPU ( vllm-torchtpu ), a new backend for running vLLM on Google Cloud TPUs. It's built on Google's TorchTPU stack and runs the model definitions that already live in vLLM, so most models that work in vLLM today can be served on TPU without changes to the model code. This work comes out of the engineering partnership between Inferact and Google we announced last month. Our goals for the project are to: vllm-torchtpu is an out-of-tree vLLM platform plugin. Once installed, vLLM picks it up automatically through the vllm.platform_plugins entry point. Models run through vLLM's standard model runner and are compiled with torch.compile(backend="tpu") , which lowers to XLA. Each TPU device gets its own worker process, the same way vLLM runs on GPUs, and communication between devices goes through torch.distributed . This means the scheduler, workers, KV cache manager, and API server are all unmodified upstream vLLM. The TPU-specific work sits underneath them, mostly in a set of JAX/Pallas kernels that are registered as custom ops and called from inside the compiled graph. This requires Python 3.12 on a Cloud TPU VM, and installs a matching vLLM, torch , torch_tpu , and libtpu alongside the plugin. The installation guide also covers uv , source builds, and Docker . The first startup compiles TPU graphs for the configured shapes, which can take a few minutes. Set VLLM_XLA_CACHE_PATH to reuse compiled artifacts across restarts (see Compilation & Warmup Cache ). Speculative decoding, prefix caching, multi-LoRA, structured outputs, and multimodal inputs are all enabled with the usual vLLM flags. See the quickstart for more examples, including offline batch inference, multimodal models, and multi-LoRA. vllm-torchtpu uses custom Pallas kernels for complex operations that benefit from hand-tuning on TPU. Some examples: We've focused heavily on the workloads that put the most pressure on serving systems today, especially multi-turn agentic and multimodal traffic, where contexts keep growing and tool outputs can be long. All six of vLLM's parallelism dimensions are supported, on both single-host and multi-host TPU slices, and they can be combined: For large MoE models, we usually get the best throughput from data-parallel attention with expert parallelism (for example, DP=8, TP=1 with EP on a single v7x host). This keeps attention local to each device and spreads the experts across the whole slice. For long contexts, PCP and DCP split prefill
